reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Also known as Hamman-Rich syndrome; a fulminant idiopathic interstitial pneumonia.
Presents like the acute respiratory distress syndrome but without an identifiable cause, frequently after a viral-like prodrome.
Rapidly progressive breathlessness and hypoxaemic respiratory failure evolve over days to a few weeks.
HRCT shows bilateral ground-glass opacity and consolidation, often diffuse, with traction bronchiectasis emerging in the organising phase.
Histology demonstrates diffuse alveolar damage, the same pattern seen in the acute respiratory distress syndrome.

It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring the ruling out of infection, sepsis, drugs, aspiration, connective tissue disease, acute eosinophilic pneumonia and acute exacerbation of pre-existing interstitial lung disease.
Management is largely supportive with lung-protective ventilation; corticosteroids are often given although supporting evidence is weak.
reference.pathophysiology: Acute interstitial pneumonia is the idiopathic form of diffuse alveolar damage. Acute injury to the alveolar-capillary membrane produces an exudative phase with interstitial and alveolar oedema and hyaline membranes, followed by an organising or proliferative phase with fibroblast proliferation and alveolar septal thickening. The absence of an identifiable trigger distinguishes it from the acute respiratory distress syndrome of known cause.
additionalDifferentials: Acute respiratory distress syndrome from infection or sepsis
Acute exacerbation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or other interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: HRCT thorax to define the extent and phase of alveolar damage
Bronchoalveolar lavage to exclude infection, haemorrhage and eosinophilia
Comprehensive microbiology including atypical and viral pathogens
Echocardiography to exclude cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Surgical lung biopsy where feasible to confirm diffuse alveolar damage and exclude mimics
redFlags: Failure to identify a reversible or treatable cause
reference.prognosis: Mortality is high, often exceeding half of patients in the acute phase; survivors may regain normal lung function or develop residual fibrosis, and recurrence has been described.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude treatable infection before attributing the illness to acute interstitial pneumonia
Missing an acute exacerbation of previously undiagnosed underlying interstitial lung disease
Overlooking diffuse alveolar haemorrhage or acute eosinophilic pneumonia, which are treatable

management: Lung-protective mechanical ventilation with low tidal volumes and supplemental oxygen for hypoxaemic respiratory failure
Empirical high-dose systemic corticosteroids, given the underlying diffuse alveolar damage, once mimics are excluded
Broad empirical antimicrobial cover until infection is excluded by bronchoalveolar lavage and microbiology
Exclude and treat mimics including sepsis, drug reactions, aspiration, and connective tissue disease
Intensive care support with consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in refractory hypoxaemia
Monitor for progression to fibrosis and consider lung transplantation assessment in survivors with residual disease
Multidisciplinary management with respiratory medicine, radiology, and intensive care
